messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Drug Use: take drugs, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Khang was thirty-one years old, a carpenter who had spent the last decade building custom shelving and cabinetry for new homes in the suburbs of Portland. He was married to a woman named Linh, a nurse who worked twelve-hour shifts, and they lived in a small bungalow with a backyard garden he had built himself. He had come to therapy at his wife’s insistence, six months after the incident, and he sat in the chair with his hands clasped so tightly that his knuckles were white. He had not planned to tell anyone about what happened, but Linh had found him one night in the garage, sitting in the dark with his back pressed against the wall, and she had not let it go.

The event itself had taken place on a Tuesday afternoon in late March. Khang had been driving home from a job site, his truck bed full of scrap wood and a half-finished set of shelves he was building for a client. He had stopped at a gas station off Highway 26 to fill up, and while he was inside paying, a man had walked in and tried to rob the register. Khang had not seen the man’s face, only the gun, and he had dropped to the floor behind a rack of chips. But when the police arrived, they had not known who he was. They had seen a Southeast Asian man in a hooded jacket crouched behind a display, and they had screamed at him to show his hands. He had done exactly what they said, but they had still tackled him, had still pressed his face into the linoleum, had still put a knee in his back while handcuffing him. He had not been charged with anything. The robbery had been caught on camera, and the cashier had told them he was a customer. But the officers had not apologized. One of them had said, “You should have stayed on the ground,” as if he had done something wrong.

In the months that followed, Khang had come to believe that the whole thing was his fault. He told himself that if he had just stayed in his truck, if he had not gone inside, if he had driven to a different gas station, none of it would have happened. He replayed the moment over and over in his head, not the robbery itself but the sound of the officers’ boots on the tile and the way his own voice had cracked when he tried to explain. He had started smoking marijuana in the evenings, then in the afternoons, then before any job that required him to drive past a gas station. He had also begun to avoid thinking about it entirely, pushing the memory away whenever it surfaced, but it always came back, unbidden, in the quiet moments.

The most immediate consequence was that he could no longer relax. Even at home, even with Linh asleep beside him, he felt a low-grade vigilance that never turned off. He had developed a specific habit: he would not sit or stand anywhere that did not have a wall behind him. In the workshop, he had repositioned his workbench so that his back faced the brick wall and he could see the entire room. At restaurants, he insisted on the booth farthest from the door. At home, he sat on the couch in a way that allowed him to see both the front and back entrances. He was certain that if he could not see a threat coming, it would catch him off guard, and he would not survive it. He also found himself unable to tolerate any kind of delay. If a client did not call him back within the hour, he assumed they had reported him for something, or that the police were on their way. If Linh was late coming home from the hospital, he would stand in the kitchen with his back to the wall and wait, his heart racing, until he heard her key in the lock.

The avoidance had begun to affect his work. He had stopped taking jobs that required him to drive through certain neighborhoods, which meant turning down a third of his usual contracts. He had also stopped going to the hardware store on weekends, sending his apprentice instead, because the store was near the gas station. His income had dropped, and he had started to tell Linh that he was just tired, that the carpentry was getting harder on his body. But what frightened him most was the feeling that he was never safe, even when he knew he was safe. He could be standing in his own backyard, with the fence locked and Linh inside, and he would still feel a pressure behind his ribs, a readiness to run.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in the garage three weeks ago. He had been sanding a piece of oak, and the radio had been playing a song he did not recognize, and suddenly he had felt the weight of a knee on his back again, so vividly that he had dropped the sandpaper and pressed himself against the wall. He had stayed there for forty minutes, unable to move, until Linh came home and found him. She had sat down next to him on the concrete floor, and she had said, “Khang, this is not going to fix itself.” He had agreed to come to therapy, but he was not sure what he hoped for. He was afraid that talking about it would make it real again, and he was afraid that if he stopped being vigilant, something terrible would happen. But he was also tired of living with his back to the wall.
